                                                   LIPSCHITZ-FREE SPACES AND BOSSARD’S REDUCTION
                                                                     ARGUMENT

                                                                                    RICHARD J. SMITH


                                                   Abstract. We set up a descriptive set-theoretic framework to study Lipschitz-free
                                                   spaces and use the reduction argument of Bossard to prove several results. We prove




arXiv:2509.00722v4 [math.FA] 23 Feb 2026
                                                   two universality results: if a separable Banach space is isomorphically universal for the
                                                   class of Lipschitz-free spaces over the countable complete discrete metric spaces then it
                                                   is isomorphically universal for the class of separable Banach spaces, and if a complete
                                                   separable metric space is Lipschitz universal for the same class of metric spaces then
                                                   it is Lipschitz universal for all separable metric spaces. We also show that there exist
                                                   countable complete discrete metric spaces whose Lipschitz-free spaces fail the bounded
                                                   approximation property and are thus not isomorphic to any dual Banach space. Finally,
                                                   we calculate the descriptive complexity of the classes of separable Banach spaces and
                                                   separable Lipschitz-free spaces having the approximation property.




                                                                                    1. Introduction
                                              Let M be a metric space with a base point denoted by 0. Let Lip0 (M ) denote the
                                           Banach space of real-valued Lipschitz functions that vanish at 0, endowed with the norm
                                           that assigns to each f ∈ Lip0 (M ) its optimal Lipschitz constant. Recall that the map
                                           δ : M → Lip0 (M )∗ given by ⟨f, δ(x)⟩ = f (x), x ∈ M , f ∈ Lip0 (M ), is an isometric
                                           embedding, and that we can define the Lipschitz-free space (hereafter free space) F(M )
                                           over M as the closed linear span of the image δ(M ) ⊆ Lip0 (M )∗ (where δ(M \ {0}) is
                                           linearly independent).
                                              For essential information on the fundamental properties of free spaces, we refer the
                                           reader to [17, 30]; in the latter they are known as Arens-Eells spaces. Free spaces have
                                           close ties to metric geometry, optimal transport theory and the linear and non-linear theory
                                           of Banach spaces, and have been the subject of intense study by the functional analysis
                                           community in the last two decades. Despite the ease with which they can be defined and
                                           the considerable progress made in understanding them over the intervening years, their
                                           structure is still relatively poorly understood and lots of “elementary” questions about
                                           them persist unanswered.
                                              One of the enduring themes of this research has been to find conditions on metric spaces
                                           to decide whether their corresponding free spaces are linearly isomorphic or not. If M is
                                           Lipschitz isomorphic to a subspace of N then F(M ) is linearly isomorphic to a subspace
                                           of F(N ), and if M and N are Lipschitz isomorphic then F(M ) and F(N ) are linearly
                                           isomorphic. However, the converses to these statements fail dramatically. In particular, it
                                           is not easy to find families of metric spaces whose corresponding free spaces are pairwise
                                           non-isomorphic.
                                              Date: February 24, 2026.
                                              2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary 46B20; Secondary 03E15.
                                              Key words and phrases. Lipschitz-free space, universality, descriptive set theory, approximation prop-
                                           erty, bounded approximation property.
                                                                                              1
2                                        R. J. SMITH


   The first example of an uncountable family of separable metric spaces whose free spaces
are pairwise non-isomorphic was given in [20]. These metric spaces are all homeomorphic
to the Cantor set 2ω . Two more uncountable families of this kind are given in [3, 4]. In
[3], each metric space in the family is countable and complete, while in [4] each one is
countable complete and discrete. The free spaces corresponding to the first family are
non-isomorphic because the weak-fragmentability (or weak Szlenk) index of each one is
distinct (and countable). The same holds in the case of the second family, this time with
respect to the dentability index (not to be confused with the w∗ -dentability index).
   These results have consequences for universality. Recall that a metric space is purely
1-unrectifiable (p1u) if and only if it admits no Lipschitz isomorphic copy of any compact
subset of R having strictly positive Lebesgue measure [23]. By [1], a complete separable
metric space M is p1u if and only if F(M ) has the Radon-Nikodým property (RNP);
equivalently the dentability index of F(M ) is countable. Because the dentability index
of each free space associated with the second family is distinct, the set of indices must
be unbounded in ω1 . Thus, if a complete separable metric space has a free space that
is isomorphically universal for the class of free spaces over countable complete discrete
metric spaces, it cannot be p1u. Consequently, if a complete separable metric space is
Lipschitz universal for the class of countable complete discrete metric spaces, it cannot be
p1u [4, Corollary 4.7].
   In this paper we use a tool from descriptive set theory, specifically Bossard’s reduction
argument (see [10, p. 31]), to build on this universality result.
Theorem 1.1. Let X be a separable Banach space that is isomorphically universal for the
class of free spaces over countable complete discrete metric spaces. Then X is isomorphi-
cally universal for the class of separable Banach spaces.
Theorem 1.2. Let M be a complete separable metric space that is Lipschitz universal for
the class of countable complete discrete metric spaces. Then M is Lipschitz universal for
the class of separable metric spaces.
   Another enduring strand of this research has been to identify which free spaces have or
fail one of Grothendieck’s classical approximation properties. Recall that a Banach space
X is said to have the approximation property (AP) if, given compact K ⊆ X and ε > 0,
there exists a bounded linear finite-rank operator T : X → X such that ∥T x − x∥ ⩽ ε
whenever x ∈ K. If there exists λ ⩾ 1 such that the operator T can always be chosen to
satisfy ∥T ∥ ⩽ λ, then X is said to have the λ-bounded approximation property (λ-BAP).
We say that X has the bounded approximation property (BAP) if it has the λ-BAP for
some λ, and the metric approximation property (MAP) if it has the 1-BAP.
   The literature on free spaces and approximation properties is too abundant to be sum-
marised in this short paper; we invite the interested reader to consult [18] and the intro-
duction of [24] and references therein for more information. We only need to recall two
results for our purposes. First, it follows immediately from [17, Theorem 3.1] that if a
separable Banach space X fails the AP then so does F(X). Second, [2, Corollary 2.8]
implies that F(M ) has the AP whenever M is countable discrete and complete. To the
best of my knowledge, to date there has been no example of a complete separable p1u
metric space whose free space has the AP but fails the BAP. The next result shows that
there are such examples and, moreover, they can be chosen to be countable complete and
discrete. Again, this result is based on Bossard’s argument. Another crucial ingredient is
the fact that, relative to the established descriptive set-theoretic frameworks for separable
              LIPSCHITZ-FREE SPACES AND BOSSARD’S REDUCTION ARGUMENT                         3


Banach spaces (see Section 2), the class of separable Banach spaces that satisfies the BAP
is Borel (though being analytic would have sufficed) [16].

Theorem 1.3. There exist countable complete discrete metric spaces M such that F(M )
fails the BAP. Consequently, F(M ) is not isomorphic to a dual space.

   This result can be contrasted with [1, Theorem 3.2] which states, among other things,
that F(M ) is isometric to a dual space whenever M is a p1u metric space that is proper,
i.e. its closed balls are compact. It can also be regarded in the light of Kalton’s problem
of whether F(M ) has the BAP whenever M is uniformly discrete; see [21, p. 185] and
e.g. [18, Problem 4.1] for more context. In this vein, there exists a uniformly discrete space
whose free space is not isometric to a dual space (though this particular example has the
MAP) [15, Example 5.8].
   We prove the results above using Lemma 3.10, which is one of our two main tools.
The other main tool, Lemma 3.9, will be needed for our final main result, Theorem 4.1,
which shows that the classes of separable Banach spaces and separable free spaces having
the AP are, relative to the appropriate descriptive set-theoretic interpretations, complete
coanalytic sets. (We remark that this is not the first time Polish spaces of metrics have
been used to study free spaces and approximation properties; see [25–27].)
   We prove these theorems in Sections 3 and 4, and make some related observations along
the way. The application of descriptive set theory to Banach space theory can be traced
to some seminal papers of Bourgain, e.g. [6]. It was formalised later by Bossard in another
seminal paper [5] and has since developed into a rich and beautiful subfield that boasts
many powerful techniques and results, see e.g. [10] and references therein, and [8] and
related papers for more recent developments. I speculate that techniques from descriptive
set theory could be used to prove more results about free spaces in the future.
   I heard about the results in [4] in a talk given by E. Basset at the Banff International
Research Station workshop on Functional and Metric Analysis and their Interactions, held
at the Institute of Mathematics, University of Granada, Spain, in May 2025. It occurred to
me that it might be possible to use descriptive set theory, specifically Bossard’s reduction
argument (see [10, p. 31]), to build on their universality results. I would like to thank
E. Basset, G. Lancien and A. Procházka for the fascinating exchanges that ensued. In
particular, Theorem 1.2 was prompted by a question asked by G. Lancien. I would also
like to thank M. Cúth, G. Godefroy and A. Rueda Zoca for several remarks which helped
me when I was preparing this paper. Finally, I should stress that I have left out most of the
results in [3, 4] from this introduction purely in the interests of brevity, and I recommend
that the interested reader should consult these papers in full.


                            2. Notation and preliminaries
   We use standard Banach space notation throughout. The closed unit ball of a Banach
space X is denoted BX . Given Banach spaces X and Y , we write X ,→ Y and X ≡ Y when
X is linearly isomorphic to a subspace of Y and X is linearly isometric to Y , respectively.
We also use these symbols in the context of metric spaces M and N , with “Lipschitz”
substituted for “linear”. By [30, Theorems 3.6 and 3.7], if M ,→ N (in the Lipschitz
sense) then F(M ) ,→ F(N ) (in the linear sense). We say that the Banach space X is
isomorphically universal for a given class C of Banach spaces if Y ,→ X whenever Y ∈ C;
Lipschitz universality of metric spaces is defined analogously.
4                                         R. J. SMITH


    For concepts pertaining to descriptive set theory, we follow [22]. The sets of natural
numbers, countable ordinals and infinite sequences of natural numbers are denoted ω, ω1
and ω ω , respectively. We identify the power set of a set Γ with 2Γ . We denote by Σ0α
and Π0α the additive and multiplicative Borel classes of order α < ω1 in a Polish space,
so that Fσ , Gδ and Fσδ -sets are Σ02 , Π02 and Π03 -sets, and so on. Analytic, coanalytic and
Borel subsets of Polish spaces are called Σ11 , Π11 and ∆11 -sets, respectively. Given subsets
A ⊆ X, B ⊆ Y of Polish spaces X and Y , we say that A is reducible to B if there is a
continuous function f : X → Y such that A = f −1 (B). If Γ(X) is a class of subsets of
a Polish space X, a subset B ⊆ Y of a Polish space Y is called Γ-hard if A is reducible
to B whenever A ∈ Γ(X) and X is Polish and zero-dimensional, and Γ-complete if B is
Γ-hard and in addition belongs to Γ(Y ).
    The tree of finite (possibly empty) sequences of natural numbers is denoted ω <ω . Given
s, t ∈ ω <ω and n ∈ ω, we define |s| = dom s ∈ ω and s⌢ n = s ∪ {(|s|, n)}, we write
s ≼ t when t is an extension of s, i.e. s = t↾|s| , and s ⊥ t when s, t are incomparable,
and finally we let s ∧ t denote the greatest element of ω <ω less than both s and t. The
space of trees, i.e. downwards-closed subsets of ω <ω , is denoted Tr. With respect to the
                                          <ω
pointwise topology this is closed in 2ω and hence compact. Within Tr we consider the
subsets WF and IF of well-founded and ill-founded trees, which are well-known to be Π11
and Σ11 -complete, respectively.
    Next, we set up an appropriate descriptive set-theoretic framework for the class of
separable infinite-dimensional free spaces. We shall consider the Polish space [0, ∞)ω×ω
endowed with the pointwise topology, and the set R ⊆ [0, ∞)ω×ω of metrics on ω. This
space was introduced by Vershik in [28] and features again in e.g. [29] and [7] (in these works
R is defined instead as the set of all pseudo-metrics on ω, that is, functions d ∈ [0, ∞)ω×ω
that are metrics except that it is possible to have distinct i, j ∈ ω satisfying d(i, j) = 0).
It is easily seen that R is a Gδ in [0, ∞)ω×ω and is thus Polish as well. This space can
be used to code the class of complete separable infinite metric spaces. Given such a
space (M, ρ), fix a dense sequence of distinct points (xi ) ⊆ M and consider d ∈ R given
by d(i, j) = ρ(xi , xj ), i, j ∈ ω; then (M, ρ) ≡ Md , where Md is the completion of (ω, d).
Conversely any such completion is separable and infinite. Because a free space is separable
and infinite-dimensional if and only if its underlying metric space is separable and infinite,
and because the free space over a metric space is isometric to that of its completion, R
can be seen as a natural coding of the class of separable infinite-dimensional free spaces.
As a change of base point does not alter the isometric structure of the corresponding free
space, we shall always regard 0 ∈ ω as the base point.
    Bossard coded the class of separable infinite-dimensional Banach spaces as a ∆11 subset
SB of the set of closed subsets of C(2ω ) equipped with the Effros-Borel structure. Following
a programme initiated in [19], the authors of [8, 9] (and related papers) observed that it
is possible to code the class of separable infinite-dimensional Banach spaces using an
arguably canonical Polish space B. First they let V be the countable Q-linear vector
space of elements of c00 having rational entries, and then they define B to be the set of
all functions µ ∈ [0, ∞)V which can be extended (uniquely) to a norm on c00 . Endowed
with the pointwise topology, B is a Gδ in [0, ∞)V and is thus Polish. Every separable
and infinite-dimensional Banach space (X, ∥·∥) has representatives inP     B. Given a linearly
independent sequence (xi ) ⊆ X having dense span, define µ(v) =             i∈ω v(i)xi , where
v ∈ V . Then X ≡ Xµ , where Xµ is the completion of (V, µ); conversely, every such
completion is a separable and infinite-dimensional Banach space. We will work with B
              LIPSCHITZ-FREE SPACES AND BOSSARD’S REDUCTION ARGUMENT                               5


instead of SB because, in our opinion, it is easier to use and more compatible with R.
While not directly relevant to this paper, another advantage of using B is that Baire
category arguments can be applied, e.g. the set of µ ∈ B such that Xµ ≡ G, where G
is the Gurariı̆ space, is a dense Gδ [8, Theorem 4.1], hence G can be thought of as the
generic separable Banach space. According to [9, Theorem 8], there is a Borel isomorphism
Θ : B → SB such that Θ(µ) ≡ Xµ for all µ ∈ B. It follows easily from this and [5, Theorem
2.3 (ii)] that, given any separable Banach space X, the set ⟨X⟩B  ,→ := {µ ∈ B : Xµ ,→ X}
is Σ11 .
   Concerning Polish versus Effros-Borel structures, we should mention that it is possible
to code the class of complete infinite separable metric spaces using the set of closed infinite
subsets of the Urysohn universal separable metric space U, again equipped with the Effros-
Borel structure, see e.g. [13, 14]. However we shall work with Vershik’s space R for the
reasons given above. Also, analogously to G, the set of d ∈ R such that Md ≡ U is a dense
Gδ [29, Theorems 1 and 3]. Thus F(U), called the Holmes space in [12], could be regarded
as the generic separable free space. An immediate consequence of this and [12, Theorem
2.1] is that the set of d ∈ R for which F(Md ) has the metric approximation property is
residual. This observation complements Theorem 4.1.

                                  3. Three main results
  Our first result will allow us to apply to R one of the observations about B recorded
above.
Proposition 3.1. There is a continuous map Ξ : R → B such that XΞ(d) ≡ F(Md ) for
all d ∈ R.

   Next, we determine the descriptive complexity of the classes of countably infinite com-
plete discrete metric spaces and complete separable p1u metric spaces.
Proposition 3.3. The set Rdis := {d ∈ R : Md is discrete} is Π11 .
Proof. It is clear that d ∈ Rdis if and only if every Cauchy sequence in (ω, d) is eventually
constant. Given k, m ∈ ω, define the sets

eventually constant. Therefore R\Rdis is Σ11 because it is the image of A\(R×B) ⊆ R×ω ω
under the projection onto the first coordinate.                                              □
Proposition 3.4. The set Rp1u := {d ∈ R : Md is p1u} is Π11 .
Proof. Using the Borel isomorphism Θ : B → SB and [5, Corollary 3.3], the set of µ ∈ B
such that Xµ has the RNP is Π11 . Now apply Proposition 3.1 and [1, Theorem 4.6].    □
   Proposition 3.4 can be proved more directly using Kirchheim’s characterisation of p1u
spaces mentioned above. Later, in Proposition 3.13, we upgrade Rdis and Rp1u to Π11 -
complete. For this and the main results we will need the following lemma, which is a tool
for generating continuous maps from power sets to R.

Lemma 3.5. Let (M, d) be a metric space, A ⊆ ω, ϕ0 : A → M and ϕ1 , ϕ2 : ω \ A → M
injections with pairwise disjoint ranges, and let τ : ω \ A → Γ, where Γ is a set. Then the
map Ψ : 2Γ → M ω given by
                            
                            ϕ0 (n) if n ∈ A,
                            
                Ψ(E)(n) = ϕ1 (n) if n ∈ ω \ A and τ (n) ∈    / E, E ∈ 2Γ ,
                            
                              ϕ2 (n) if n ∈ ω \ A and τ (n) ∈ E,
                            

is continuous. Moreover, the map ∆ : 2Γ → [0, ∞)ω×ω given by
                     ∆(E)(m, n) = d(Ψ(E)(m), Ψ(E)(n)),                m, n ∈ ω,
is continuous and takes values in R. Finally, (ω, ∆(E)) is isometric to (Ψ(E)(ω), d).
Proof. To check continuity of Ψ, let E ∈ 2Γ and let F ⊆ ω be finite. Define the finite sets
G = τ (F \ A) ∩ E and H = τ (F \ A) \ E; then G ⊆ E, H ∩ E = ∅ and Ψ(E ′ )(n) = Ψ(E)(n)
whenever n ∈ F , E ′ ∈ 2Γ , G ⊆ E ′ and H ∩ E ′ = ∅. Therefore Ψ is continuous. As ∆ is
the composition of Ψ and another continuous map, it is also continuous. Since ϕ0 , ϕ1 , ϕ2
are injective and have pairwise disjoint ranges, Ψ(E) is injective for all E ∈ 2Γ . It follows
that ∆(E) ∈ R. The last assertion is obvious.                                               □
Remark 3.6. It is a simple exercise to show that Rcpt := {d ∈ R : Md is compact}
is Π03 . As a straightforward application, we can show that Rcpt is Π03 -complete using
Lemma 3.5. Indeed, let
             P = E ∈ 2ω×ω : {j ∈ ω : (i, j) ∈ E} is finite for all i ∈ ω .
                  

According to [22, Exercise 23.1], P is Π03 -complete. Now set Γ = ω × ω, M = ℓ1 (Γ ∪ {∞}),
A = {0} and ϕ0 = {(0, 0)}. Let d be the usual metric on M , let τ : ω \ A → Γ be a
bijection, let (eγ )γ∈Γ∪{∞} be the usual basis, and define injections ϕ1 , ϕ2 : ω \ A → M by
                      ϕ1 (n) = 2−n e∞     and ϕ2 (n) = 2−p(τ (n)) eτ (n) ,
where p : ω × ω → ω is the projection onto the first coordinate. Evidently the ranges
of ϕ0 , ϕ1 , ϕ2 are pairwise disjoint. Let ∆ be the map furnished by Lemma 3.5. Then it
is straightforward to check that M∆(E) = (ω, ∆(E)) always, and this space is compact
whenever E ∈ P and not compact otherwise. Therefore ∆ is a continuous reduction of P
to Rcpt , which implies that the latter is Π03 -complete as claimed. The precise complexity
of a few other standard classes of complete separable metric spaces can be determined in
a similar manner.
  We will be interested in metrics ρ on ω <ω satisfying the following property.
       Given ε > 0 and an infinite branch B ⊆ ω <ω , there exists n ∈ ω such that
       ρ(s, t) < ε whenever s, t ∈ B and |s|, |t| ⩾ n.                                   (3.2)
  In the next result and a number of others, M shall denote the completion of the metric
space M .
Lemma 3.7. Let M = (M, θ) be a complete separable metric space, let (xi )i∈ω be a dense
sequence in M whose elements repeat infinitely often, let ρ be a metric on ω <ω satisfying
(3.2) and define a second metric η on ω <ω by
                               η(s, t) = ρ(s, t) + θ(x|s| , x|t| ).
8                                                R. J. SMITH


Then whenever T ∈ IF and B ⊆ T is an infinite branch, there exists an isometric em-
bedding ϕ : M → (B, η) ⊆ (T, η). Moreover, if M is complete then there is a 1-Lipschitz
retraction r : (T, η) → ϕ(M ).
Proof. Let q ∈ ω ω such that B = {q↾n : n ∈ ω}. We define an isometric embedding
ϕ : M → (B, η) as follows. Given x ∈ M , because the elements of (xi ) repeat infinitely
often, there exist i0 < i1 < i2 < . . . such that θ(xik , x) → 0. Given that ρ satisfies (3.2),
(q↾ik ) is ρ-Cauchy, hence (q↾ik ) is also η-Cauchy. Let ϕ(x) = limk q↾ik ∈ (B, η). This is
well-defined because if j0 < j1 < j2 < . . . also satisfy θ(xjk , x) → 0 then η(q↾ik , q↾jk ) =
ρ(q↾ik , q↾jk ) + θ(xik , xjk ) → 0, again by (3.2). Next, we check that ϕ is an isometric
embedding. With x and the ik as above, let y ∈ M and this time let j0 < j1 < j2 < . . .
such that θ(y, xjk ) → 0. Then once more by (3.2),
         η(ϕ(x), ϕ(y)) = lim η(q↾ik , q↾jk ) = lim ρ(q↾ik , q↾jk ) + θ(xik , xjk ) = θ(x, y).
                              k                          k
Finally, assume M is complete. Define ζ : T → M by ζ(s) = x|s| . This map is 1-Lipschitz
because θ(ζ(s), ζ(t)) = θ(x|s| , x|t| ) ⩽ η(s, t), s, t ∈ T . Let r : (T, η) → (B, η) be the
1-Lipschitz extension of ϕ ◦ ζ to (T, η). By the continuity of r and the completeness of
M , we have r((T, η)) ⊆ ϕ(M ). Moreover r(ϕ(x)) = ϕ(x) whenever x ∈ M . Indeed,
given i0 < i1 < i2 < . . . such that θ(xik , x) → 0, we have ϕ(x) = limk q↾ik , so r(ϕ(x)) =
limk ϕ(ζ(q↾ik )) = limk ϕ(xik ) = ϕ(x).                                                    □
   If (M, θ) above is perfect then there is no need to insist that the elements of (xi ) repeat
infinitely often.
   We now define a metric ρ on ω <ω that we fix hereafter. Let (es )s∈ω<ω denote the usual
basis of c00 (ω <ω ) and define the injection Ω : ω <ω → c00 (ω <ω ) by
                                         X
                                 Ω(s) =      2−|r| er , s ∈ ω <ω .
                                               r≼s

Then define ρ(s, t) = ∥Ω(s) − Ω(t)∥∞ , s, t ∈ ω <ω . We see that ρ satisfies (3.2). If s ⊥ t
then s ∧ t ≺ s, t and
                                   X                         X
                  ρ(s, t) =                 2−|r| er −             2−|r| er       = 2−|s∧t|−1 ,   (3.3)
                                  s∧t≺r≼s                s∧t≺r≼t              ∞
and we get the same expression for ρ(s, t) if s and t are distinct and comparable. Hence
(3.2) holds.
Lemma 3.8. Let η be the metric from Lemma 3.7, where (M, θ) is an arbitrary separable
metric space and ρ is as above. Then (ω <ω , η) is discrete, and in addition (T, η) is complete
whenever T ∈ WF.
Proof. Fix s ∈ ω <ω . Given t ∈ ω <ω \ {s}, by (3.3) we have
                              η(s, t) ⩾ ρ(s, t) = 2−|s∧t|−1 ⩾ 2−|s|−1 .
Hence η(s, t) ⩾ 2−|s|−1 whenever t ∈ ω <ω \ {s}, meaning that η is discrete.
   Now let T ∈ WF and let (sn ) ⊆ T be η-Cauchy. We find a strictly increasing finite
sequence r0 ≺ r1 ≺ r2 ≺ . . . of elements of ω <ω and infinite subsets L0 ⊇ L1 ⊇ L2 ⊇ . . .
of ω such that rk ≼ sn for all n ∈ Lk . Begin by setting r0 = ∅ and L0 = ω. Given rk
and Lk , either there exists m ∈ ω and an infinite subset Lk+1 ⊆ Lk such that rk⌢ m ≼ sn
for all n ∈ Lk+1 , or not. If the first case holds, set rk+1 = rk⌢ m and continue the process,
              LIPSCHITZ-FREE SPACES AND BOSSARD’S REDUCTION ARGUMENT                        9


else terminate it. Because T ∈ WF, this process must terminate at some finite stage k.
By construction we know that Lk is infinite and rk ≼ sn for all n ∈ Lk but also, given
m ∈ ω, the set Hm := {n ∈ Lk : rk⌢ m ≼ sn } must be finite. If n1 ∈ Hm1 and n2 ∈ Hm2
for distinct m1 , m2 ∈ ω, then sn1 ⊥ sn2 and sn1 ∧ sn2 = rk , giving
                            η(sn1 , sn2 ) ⩾ ρ(sn1 , sn2 ) = 2−|rk |−1 .
Because (sn ) is η-Cauchy, it follows that Hm is empty for all but finitely many m ∈ ω,
and thus sn = rk for infinitely many n ∈ Lk . Again because (sn ) is η-Cauchy, we conclude
that it must converge to rk . This proves that (T, η) is complete.                      □
  We make use of the last three lemmas in the next result. Lemmas 3.9 and 3.10 below
are our main tools.
Lemma 3.9. Let M = (M, θ) be a complete separable metric space. There exists a
continuous map ∆ : Tr → R such that ∆(T ) ∈ Rdis whenever T ∈ WF and M is
isometric to a 1-Lipschitz retract of M∆(T ) whenever T ∈ IF.
Proof. Let (ω <ω , η) be the metric space obtained from Lemma 3.7 applied to M . Let
W = ω <ω ∪ (ω <ω × {0}). We extend η to a metric on W , again labelled η, by setting
                                 
                                 
                                 0                   / ω <ω , x = y,
                                              if x, y ∈
                                                      / ω <ω , x ̸= y,
                                 
                                 1           if x, y ∈
                       η(x, y) =
                                 
                                 1 + η(∅, x) if x ∈ ω <ω , y ∈/ ω <ω ,
                                 
                                  1 + η(∅, y) if x ∈/ ω , y ∈ ω <ω .
                                                       <ω
                                 

It is routine to verify that this extension satisfies the triangle inequality.
   Set A = ϕ0 = ∅, Γ = ω <ω , let τ : ω → Γ be a bijection, and define injections
ϕ1 , ϕ2 : ω → W by ϕ1 (n) = (τ (n), 0) and ϕ2 (n) = τ (n), n ∈ ω. Let ∆ : 2Γ → R be the
continuous map furnished by Lemma 3.5, which we then restrict to Tr. We observe that
Ψ(T )(ω) = T ∪ ((ω <ω \ T ) × {0}) for all T ∈ Tr.
   Let T ∈ WF. Using Lemma 3.8, (T, η) is discrete and complete. Hence (ω, ∆(T )),
which is isometric to (Ψ(T )(ω), η), is also discrete and complete because every point in
(ω <ω \ T ) × {0} is η-separated from everything else by at least 1. Therefore ∆(T ) ∈ Rdis .
   Now let T ∈ IF. We claim that M is isometric to a 1-Lipschitz retract of M∆(T ) . First
of all, the function r′ : Ψ(T )(ω) → T , defined by
                                            (
                                     ′        x if x ∈ T,
                                    r (x) =
                                              ∅ if x ∈  / T,
is a 1-Lipschitz retraction of (Ψ(T )(ω), η) onto (T, η). We extend this to a 1-Lipschitz
retraction r′ : (Ψ(T )(ω), η) → (T, η). According to Lemma 3.7, there is an isometric
embedding ϕ : M → (T, η) and a 1-Lipschitz retraction r : (T, η) → ϕ(M ). Therefore
r ◦ r′ : (Ψ(T )(ω), η) → ϕ(M ) is a 1-Lipschitz retraction. Since M∆(T ) ≡ (Ψ(T )(ω), η), our
claim is proved.                                                                           □
   The final lemma below uses Bossard’s reduction argument [5, Theorem 3.2]; Theorems
1.1 – 1.3 emerge as relatively straightforward consequences of it.
Lemma 3.10. Let A ⊆ R have the property that d′ ∈ A whenever d′ ∈ R and Md′ is
isometric to a 1-Lipschitz retract of Md for some d ∈ A. Assume that Rdis ∪ A is Σ11 .
Then Rdis ∪ A = R.
10                                        R. J. SMITH


Proof. Let d ∈ R. Apply Lemma 3.9 to M := Md . The assumption Rdis ∪ A is Σ11 implies
∆−1 (Rdis ∪ A) is also Σ11 . As WF ⊆ ∆−1 (Rdis ∪ A) and WF is Π11 -complete, by Suslin’s
theorem there exists T ∈ IF such that ∆(T ) ∈ Rdis ∪ A. Because T ∈ IF, Md is isometric
to a 1-Lipschitz retract of M∆(T ) . Given our assumption about A and the fact that Rdis
also enjoys this property, it follows that d ∈ Rdis ∪ A. Therefore Rdis ∪ A = R.      □

Proof of Theorem 1.3. Using [16], [9, Theorem 8] and Proposition 3.1, the set
                         RBAP := {d ∈ R : F(Md ) has the BAP}
is ∆11 . Let d′ ∈ R and d ∈ RBAP such that Md′ is isometric to a 1-Lipschitz retract of Md .
Again by [30, Theorems 3.6 and 3.7], F(Md′ ) is linearly isometric to a 1-complemented
subspace of F(Md ) and thus d′ ∈ RBAP . For a contradiction assume Rdis ⊆ RBAP . Then
RBAP = R by Lemma 3.10. However, this is false because we can pick d ∈ R such that
Md is isometric to a separable Banach space that fails the AP; as is pointed out in the
Introduction, d ∈ / RBAP by [17, Theorem 3.1].
   Now pick d ∈ Rdis \ RBAP . Again, as stated in the Introduction, F(Md ) has the AP
by [2, Corollary 2.8]. That F(Md ) cannot be isomorphic to a dual space is a simple
consequence of the classical result of Grothendieck which asserts that a separable Banach
space has the MAP whenever it has the AP and is isometric to a dual space.               □
Remark 3.11. The set Rdis \ RBAP is Π11 by Proposition 3.3 and the fact that RBAP is
∆11 . Theorem 1.3 shows that Rdis \ RBAP is non-empty. By a simple adjustment to the
argument we see moreover that Rdis \ RBAP cannot be ∆11 : if it was ∆11 then Rdis ∪ RBAP
would be as well, thus it would be equal to R by Lemma 3.10, which again is false. We
make some remarks based on this observation.

   (2) We can replace Rdis by Rp1u to show that the set Rp1u \ RBAP (which is Π11 by

   (3) While the above results show that there are many examples of complete sepa-
       rable p1u spaces whose free spaces fail the BAP, they don’t provide an explicit
       description of any of them. It could be instructive to obtain concrete examples.

leaves open.
Problem 3.12. Let M be a complete separable p1u metric space. Does there exist a
separable Banach space X such that F(M ) ,→ X ∗ ?
  We finish this section with two direct applications of Lemma 3.9.
Proposition 3.13. The sets Rdis and Rp1u are Π11 -complete.
Proof. Recall that, by Propositions 3.3 and 3.4, these sets are Π11 . Select any complete
separable non-p1u metric space M . Then the map ∆ furnished by Lemma 3.9 applied to
M witnesses the fact that WF is reducible to Rdis and Rp1u .                           □
   In the final result of this section, we obtain a lower bound on the complexity of the set
of metrics in R whose free spaces satisfy the AP. The complexity calculation is completed
in Section 4.
Proposition 3.14. The set RAP := {d ∈ R : F(Md ) has the AP} is Π11 -hard.
Proof. Apply Lemma 3.9 to a separable Banach space M that fails the AP. If T ∈ WF
then F(M∆(T ) ) has the AP again by [2, Corollary 2.8]. If T ∈ IF then M is isometric to a
1-Lipschitz retract of M∆(T ) . Once again by [30, Theorems 3.6 and 3.7], F(M ) is linearly
isometric to a 1-complemented subspace of F(M∆(T ) ). Since F(M ) fails the AP, so must
F(M∆(T ) ). Therefore ∆ witnesses the fact that WF is reducible to RAP .                 □

                  4. Complexity and the approximation property
   This section is solely concerned with determining the complexity of two classes of Banach
spaces having the AP. The proof of the result below is an adaptation of an argument from
[16]. As above, we frame the result in terms of the Polish space B instead of the Effros-
Borel space SB.
